why/node: Picture one node inside a bigger graph. It multiplies a vector, x, by a matrix, W.
why/out: Its result, z, flows on through the rest of the graph, which ends in a single number, f.
why/weights: Each entry of W is called a weight, because it weighs how much one entry of x counts toward one entry of z. This W holds six.
why/nudge: Nudge one weight, the one in row zero, column one, and f moves.
why/name: Call that weight W zero one: row zero, column one, both counted from zero.
why/grid: How far f moves per nudge of each weight is the gradient partial f, partial W: a grid shaped like W, one slope per weight, saying which way to nudge each.
why/dz: Backprop has already walked back from f to this node's output, so partial f, partial z has arrived: one number per entry of z, here two and minus one.
why/ask: In code it is called d z. From it and x, the node must work out partial f, partial W.
gate/row: Zoom in on W zero one. It sits in row zero, so it helps make only z zero, the first entry of z: row zero of W, dotted with x.
gate/gates: A dot product is a few multiplies, added up. So as a graph, each weight meets its entry of x in a multiply gate, and one add sums the three.
gate/x1: W zero one's partner is x one, entry one of x, which is four.
gate/copy: Now walk back. partial f, partial z zero, which is two, arrives at the add, and the add copies it to every multiply.
gate/swap: The multiply swaps: W zero one gets its partner's value, four, times two. Eight.
gate/row0: Its neighbors in row zero work the same way, each with its own partner from x.
gate/z1: And z one's gradient never reaches W zero one at all: that weight plays no part in z one.
gate/rule: So in general, the weight in row i, column j gets the gradient on output i, times input j.
grid/fill: Do that for every weight, and partial f, partial W fills in. Row zero is x times two: six, eight and two.
grid/row1: Row one is x times z one's gradient, which is minus one: so minus three, minus four and minus one.
grid/e10: So entry one, zero, in row one and column zero, is minus one times three: minus three. The row picks the gradient, and the column picks the input.
grid/table: Seen whole, it is a multiplication table: d z down the side, x across the top, and in each cell, its row's number times its column's.
grid/outer: It is called the outer product of d z and x. A dot product pairs two vectors inward, down to one number. The outer product spreads them out, every entry with every entry, into a table.
grid/T: As a matrix product, it is d z, x transpose: d z standing as a column, two by one, times x laid down as a row, one by three.
grid/shapes: Two by one, times one by three: the inner ones match and vanish, leaving two by three, the shape of W, as its gradient must be.
grid/flip: The other order, x times d z transpose, builds the same table on its side: three by two, which does not fit W.
grid/big: The shapes work the same at any size: a ten by three thousand and seventy two W gets a ten by three thousand and seventy two gradient.
